speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome. I am Dr. Agent. I see you are a newborn presenting with respiratory distress. To begin our evaluation, how long has the distress been present, and were there any complications during your birth, such as prematurity or infection?

speaker: Patient
text: Newborn, born at 33 weeks of gestation. The newborn is presenting with respiratory distress 2 hours after birth. The mother had an uneventful pregnancy until premature onset of labor. There was no significant prenatal care history mentioned.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Thank you for the details. Given the 33-week gestation and onset of distress within two hours of birth, is there a history of maternal chorioamnionitis, and did the baby pass meconium before delivery?

REQUEST TEST: Arterial_Blood_Gas, CBC_with_Diff.
REQUEST IMAGES: Chest_X-Ray.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Arterial Blood Gas: pH 7.30 (slightly acidic), PaCO2 50 mmHg (elevated), PaO2 60 mmHg (reduced), HCO3- 24 mEq/L; CBC with Diff: Not available in provided data; Chest X-Ray: Fine reticular granulation with ground glass appearance on both lungs.

speaker: Doctor
text: The blood gas results indicate respiratory acidosis, and the chest X-ray showing a ground-glass appearance in a premature infant is highly suggestive of Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS). Did your baby exhibit grunting, nasal flaring, or retractions during breathing?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Respiratory distress. I also have Grunting, Intercoastal and subcostal retractions, Peripheral cyanosis.

speaker: Doctor
text:
The clinical picture of respiratory distress in a 33-week premature infant, combined with ground-glass opacities on the chest X-ray, respiratory acidosis, and physical signs like grunting and retractions, is classic for Respiratory Distress Syndrome. Given the strong evidence, I have made my determination.

DIAGNOSIS READY: Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS)
